title: History from below: E. P. Thompson, the Luddites and ordinary lives

explain.say: Picture an English cloth worker in 1812, hammer in hand, smashing a new machine that has taken his job. Old books called the Luddites backward fools. In 1963 E. P. Thompson asked a different question: what did they want, and why? That question is history from below. Look at the two sides on the board.

explain.say: See the left side: history from above, written through kings, generals and state papers. The right side looks from below: workers, peasants, servants and women, using court records, parish registers, ballads and petitions. Which of these sources do you think survives most often for poor people?

explain.say: Now the timeline. Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class argued that workers made their own class through experience and struggle; it was not simply produced by factories. In a famous preface he set out to rescue the Luddite cropper and the poor stocking weaver from the condescension of later generations. Why might a failed movement still matter?

explain.say: The idea spread. In 1973 Sheila Rowbotham showed how women had been hidden from history. In 1982 Ranajit Guha launched Subaltern Studies in India, writing peasant rebels back into the story of colonial rule. Subaltern means people of lower rank, without power. Whose history in your own country is still told mostly from above?

explain.say: Critics warn that history from below can romanticise the poor, and that sources are thin, so we often hear ordinary people only through the officials who arrested or taxed them. Well done. Your challenge: find one court or parish record from your town and ask what it reveals about an ordinary life.

faq.a: History from below studies the past through the lives and actions of ordinary people, such as workers, peasants, slaves and women, rather than only rulers and elites. E. P. Thompson named it in a 1966 essay.

faq.q: What did E. P. Thompson argue in The Making of the English Working Class?
faq.a: Thompson argued, in 1963, that the English working class made itself between about 1780 and 1832 through shared experience, traditions and struggle. Class was a relationship and a process, not just a result of factories.
asks: What is The Making of the English Working Class about?

faq.a: Textile workers in northern and central England who broke machines between 1811 and 1816, protesting against wage cuts, cheap labour and new machinery that threatened their skilled trades.
asks: Why did the Luddites smash machines?

faq.a: A group of historians led by Ranajit Guha, starting in 1982, who studied peasants and other subordinated groups in South Asia, challenging both colonial and nationalist elite histories.

Women's history recovers women's experiences and roles in the past. Sheila Rowbotham's Hidden from History, 1973, was an early landmark; later gender history studied how ideas of men and women shaped every society.

facts: E. P. Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class was published in 1963.
Luddite machine breaking took place in England mainly between 1811 and 1816.
The first volume of Subaltern Studies, edited by Ranajit Guha, appeared in 1982.
